title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 23 -- fine-tuning for classification
summary: After all the hard work, chapter 6 is a nice easy one -- how do we take a next-token predictor and turn it into a classifier?
markdown:
In chapter 5 of [Sebastian Raschka](https://sebastianraschka.com/)'s book "[Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)](https://www.manning.com/books/build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch)", we finally [trained our LLM](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-22-finally-training-our-llm) (having learned essential aspects like [cross entropy loss](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-20-starting-training-cross-entropy-loss) and [perplexity](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-21-perplexed-by-perplexity) along the way). This is amazing -- we've gone from essentially zero to a full pretrained model. But pretrained models aren't all that useful in and of themselves -- we normally do further training to specialise them on a particular task, like being a chatbot.

Chapter 6 explains a -- to me -- slightly surprising thing that we can do with this kind of fine-tuning. We take our LLM and convert it into a classifier that assesses whether or not a given piece of text is spam. That's simple enough that I can cover everything in one post -- so here it is :-)

### The decapitation technique

The core idea in the chapter is the trick that we use to change an LLM that is designed to predict the next token into one that classifies texts into different categories.

What we do is remove its final layer -- the one that maps from 768-dimensional embedding space to vocab space so that we get our logits to turn into a probability distribution -- and replace it with a much simpler one, which maps from the 768-dimensional embedding space to a 2-dimensional one, where logits -- after softmax -- represent the respective probabilities of spam vs ham (non-spam). As Raschka says, it's as if we're constraining our model to having an output vocabulary of two tokens. We're replacing our output head with a classification head instead.

Because it involves removing the output head of the existing model, I'm calling it the decapitation technique. (ChatGPT tells me that it has a more prosaic name -- it's a *linear probe*.)

This was something I recognised from Jeremy Howard's [fast.ai course](https://course.fast.ai/) -- it looks like it might no longer be part of it (the trick in question has been absorbed into the library that the course uses), but I do remember doing an image classifier by removing the output head from an existing one and then training a new, simpler one to replace it.

With an LLM, there's an extra tweak; we only consider the logits provided for the last token. That makes sense; with the original head, the last token's embedding, projected into vocab space, is the predicted next token for the sequence as a whole, and it is the only one with information from all of the other tokens blended into it by the attention layers. Being the richest representation of the sequence, it's obviously the best one to check when we're trying to classify that sequence.

But that leads to another interesting thing about the training -- when we're calculating our loss, we only consider the cross-entropy loss between the logits vector for the last token and the target category. That makes sense simply because we don't have spam vs ham predictions for the shorter prefix sequences -- but also, we honestly don't care what its predictions for them might be. Which leads to the interesting possibility that they might wind up not being spam vs ham predictions at all -- the model has more "freedom" in how it uses them, so they could be anything.

### Datasets

There is a lot of data-wrangling going on in this chapter -- all of which is relatively simple, but one thing that stood out for me was that we make sure that we have the same amount of spam and ham in our training, validation and test sets. Intuitively this makes sense. If we had a training set that was (say) 95% ham and only 5% spam, then a model that was essentially this:

`def is_spam(text):     return False`

...would be right 95% of the time, which is around the accuracy of the trained model that we wind up with. But it would also be pretty useless. Making sure that we have similar amounts of both is a good way to avoid the model getting trained in a dumb direction like that.

I also spotted something a bit odd in the code that loads the different datasets in. Here it is:

    `train_loader = DataLoader(         dataset=train_dataset,         batch_size=batch_size,         shuffle=True,         num_workers=num_workers,         drop_last=True     )     val_loader = DataLoader(         dataset=val_dataset,         batch_size=batch_size,         shuffle=True,         num_workers=num_workers,         drop_last=False     )     test_loader = DataLoader(         dataset=test_dataset,         batch_size=batch_size,         shuffle=True,         num_workers=num_workers,         drop_last=False     )`

Look at those `drop_last` parameters -- they're `True` for the training set, but `False` for the others.

From the docs for PyTorch's [`DataLoader`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html#torch.utils.data.DataLoader)

> **drop\_last** (bool, *optional*) -- set to `True` to drop the last incomplete batch, if the dataset size is not divisible by the batch size. If `False` and the size of dataset is not divisible by the batch size, then the last batch will be smaller.

So: if the number of training samples isn't divisible by the batch size, and we had `drop_last` set to `False` for training data, then our last batch would have fewer items in it.

I think it makes intuitive sense that you'd want all of the batches going through during your training to be the same size. Let's imagine that we have ten items in most of our batches; loosely speaking, that means that on each gradient update, each one of those items will contribute 10% of the update. But if the last batch has only four items, then those four will each contribute 25%. So the items in the last, smaller batch will have an outsized impact on the model's training, which would obviously be a bad thing.

For our validation and test sets, it's pretty clear that it doesn't matter -- all we want to do for them is work out how good the model is at classifying them, and they don't have a direct impact on the model's parameter updates.

### The initial test

Before we start training, we see whether our model -- with its original projection-to-vocab head in place -- can classify text as spam or not. We feed it this:

```
Is the following text 'spam'?  Answer with 'yes' or 'no': 'You are a winner you
have been specifically selected to receive $1000 cash or a $2000 reward.'
```

...and it responds with this:

```
The following text 'spam'?  Answer with 'yes' or 'no': 'You are a
```

So, no luck -- not a big surprise.

Now, quite some time ago when I started playing with LLMs, I started a series trying to build an AI chatbot using the OpenAI APIs, which -- at the time -- were just text-completion based, rather than the chat-template ones that they are now. I found that even with some of the older models, you could get it to work like a chatbot by telling it what this text was meant to look like. So I tried that:

```
This is a transcript of a conversation between a helpful bot, 'Bot', and a human,
'User'.  The bot is very intelligent and always answers the human's questions
with a useful reply.

Human: Is the following text 'spam'?  Answer with 'yes' or 'no': 'You are a
winner you have been specifically selected to receive $1000 cash or a $2000 reward.'
```

Unfortunately it didn't help much -- here's what it came up with:

```
Bot:

User:

Bot:

User:

Bot:
```

Ah well, worth a try! I might give it another go once we've instruction-trained it.

So, we know we need to train our LLM -- the next bit of the book explains how to do it.

### Training and randomness

Just like [last time](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-22-finally-training-our-llm), even though Raschka uses `torch.manual_seed` in lots of places to make the results reproducible, I got different numbers to his. Interestingly, in this chapter I got pretty much the same numbers for the first few steps, but after the accuracy functions were introduced, my results started differing. Again, I don't think this matters much so long as the numbers are similar. (With the caveat of some slightly disappointing results I got at the end.)

I was interested in the trick of freezing the gradients on almost all of the LLM's layers -- only allowing the last one, and the final layer-norm to be trained, plus the new output head. It kind of reminded me of LoRA, which reduces the amount of work you need to do to fine-tune a model by limiting the number of weights you change -- though the way that works is quite different (you introduce new, smaller weight matrices that "adapt" the results of the existing frozen ones, and then train those).

Raschka suggests an exercise where you try training all of the layers -- that is, with none of them frozen. I did that, and the results were really interesting -- more on that later...

One thing that did surprise me a bit was that in this chapter we're training with [dropout](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/03/llm-from-scratch-10-dropout) of zero. It seems strange, but I think it's because we're freezing those layers. The number of parameters that are actually being trained is small, so dropping them out might just throw away signal from the training, and make it converge more slowly. What's worse is that there's nothing stopping dropout from happening in those frozen layers, too -- we've set `requires_grad` to `False`, so they're not being updated by the training loop, but the model is still in training mode, so dropout would happen in them if it wasn't set to zero.

Anyway, the code to actually run the training is pretty simple and I won't repeat what is already explained perfectly well in the book. My train (with whatever the differences with the seed it had from Raschka's) came out with broadly similar results:

```
Training accuracy: 97.12%
Validation accuracy: 95.97%
Test accuracy: 95.67%
```

It took 15 seconds on my RTX 3090 -- within the "less than half a minute" range he mentions for the V100 and A100 datacenter cards. Plotting the loss:

![Loss over time training just the last layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/last-layers-loss-plot.png "Loss over time training just the last layers")

...you can see that it looks very similar to what happens in the book.

The accuracy was kind of interesting, though:

![Accuracy over time training just the last layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/last-layers-accuracy-plot.png "Accuracy over time training just the last layers")

You can see that mine actually dropped off on the validation set near the start -- however, it did recover nicely, so no big deal. It looks like the best results were in somewhere around epoch 4, but there's not a huge drop off from there to where we stop at the end of epoch 5. [1](#fn-1)

The final results were a little disappointing, though. In the last pages of the chapter, we run two sentences through our trained classifier. Firstly, something that is very spammy:

```
You are a winner you have been specially selected to receive $1000 cash or a
$2000 reward
```

And secondly something that isn't spammy:

```
Hey, just wanted to check if we're still on for dinner tonight? Let me know!
```

Unfortunately, due to the differences in seeding between my model and the one Raschka was working with, I got the same result for both: `not spam`.

After checking the code carefully, I decided to take a look at what the actual predictions looked like; in the `classify_review` function that we write to do these tests, I added this:

`print(torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1))`

For the ham case, this printed:

```
tensor([[0.9771, 0.0229]], device='cuda:0')
```

The first element (index 0) is the probability that it is predicting for ham, and the second is the probability for spam. So it was 97% sure that the ham message was indeed ham. That's good!

For the spam message, though, it was pretty much on the fence:

```
tensor([[0.5987, 0.4013]], device='cuda:0')
```

It thought that there was a 59.87% chance that it was ham, but a 40.13% chance that it was spam. It would be interesting to know what Raschka's own train came up with, but I can imagine that it might be a similarly close-run thing, and I was just unlucky with the way the randomness in training fell out.

But I decided to try training all of the layers to see if I got any different results.

### Training all of the layers

This took 42 seconds rather than 15 -- hardly a big deal at this scale, but you can see how not having to train everything and getting a 3x speedup would be worthwhile for larger models.

The results were definitely better, though:

```
Training accuracy: 99.71%
Validation accuracy: 98.66%
Test accuracy: 97.67%
```

Maybe a little bit of overfitting going on? But the important thing is that the validation and test samples' accuracy are higher too, we're not just memorising the training set.

The loss graph also looks solid:

![Loss over time training all layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/all-layers-loss-plot.png "Loss over time training all layers")

And accuracy is really interesting:

![Accuracy over time training all layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/all-layers-accuracy-plot.png "Accuracy over time training all layers")

You can see that validation accuracy got up to 100% sometime during the first epoch, lining up with the point where the loss plateaus! Perhaps a snapshot taken then would have been the best form of the model.

But anyway, I tried running the two samples from the last pages of the chapter through this new version of the model -- the results were exactly right! "You are a winner..." was classified as spam, and "Hey, just wanted to check..." as ham. Looking at the predictions that my modification to the classification code printed out, things were even clearer. The spam had this:

```
tensor([[0.0285, 0.9715]], device='cuda:0')
```

A 97% chance that it was spam, which is excellent.

Looking at the ham message, it said this:

```
tensor([[9.9968e-01, 3.2288e-04]], device='cuda:0')
```

That's a 99.9% chance that it's ham!

So that was a nice note to end on. Not only did I have results that showed that the classification worked -- the fact that it worked with just the 30 seconds of extra training that enabling gradients on all of the layers gave meant that it was unlikely that my original slightly-disappointing results were due to an error in the code -- it was, as I'd suspected, just a bit of bad luck with some randomness.

### Wrapping up

So, that's it for chapter 6! Classification with a decapitated LLM done and dusted. Next time, it's on to instruction fine-tuning -- something that I spent quite a lot of time on [last year](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning), so let's see if all that work will pay off.

[Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-24-the-transcript-hack).

**Update**: I decided to see how easy it would be to do the same decapitation trick on a different LLM, one that I'd downloaded from Hugging Face. Turns out the answer is "[pretty easy](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/a-classifier-using-qwen3)".

* * *

1.  I've been running a number of separate experiments -- will be writing them up shortly -- in which I store a checkpoint after each validation check, and keep a symlink updated to point to the one with the best validation loss. This feels like a good practice to me. [↩](#fnref-1)

The bot is very intelligent and always answers the human's questions with a useful reply. Human: Is the following text 'spam'? Answer with 'yes' or 'no': 'You are a winner you have been specifically selected to receive $1000 cash or a $2000 reward.' ``` Unfortunately it didn't help much -- here's what it came up with: 遗憾的是，帮助不大——它生成的是： ``` Bot: User: Bot: User: Bot: ``` Ah well, worth a try! I might give it another go once we've instruction-trained it. 唉，值得一试！等我们完成指令训练后，也许可以再试一次。 So, we know we need to train our LLM -- the next bit of the book explains how to do it. 所以，我们知道需要训练 LLM——书的下一部分会解释如何做。 ### Training and randomness 训练与随机性 Just like [last time](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-22-finally-training-our-llm), even though Raschka uses `torch.manual_seed` in lots of places to make the results reproducible, I got different numbers to his. Interestingly, in this chapter I got pretty much the same numbers for the first few steps, but after the accuracy functions were introduced, my results started differing. Again, I don't think this matters much so long as the numbers are similar. (With the caveat of some slightly disappointing results I got at the end.) 和[上次](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-22-finally-training-our-llm)一样，尽管 Raschka 在很多地方使用 torch.manual_seed 来让结果可复现，我得到的数字还是不同。有趣的是，本章前几步我得到的数字几乎一样，但引入准确率函数后，结果开始出现差异。同样，只要数字相近，我不认为这很重要。（不过最后得到的一些略令人失望的结果除外。） I was interested in the trick of freezing the gradients on almost all of the LLM's layers -- only allowing the last one, and the final layer-norm to be trained, plus the new output head. It kind of reminded me of LoRA, which reduces the amount of work you need to do to fine-tune a model by limiting the number of weights you change -- though the way that works is quite different (you introduce new, smaller weight matrices that "adapt" the results of the existing frozen ones, and then train those). 我对冻结 LLM 几乎所有层的梯度这个技巧很感兴趣——只允许训练最后一层、最后的层归一化，以及新的输出头。这让我有点想起 LoRA：它通过限制要修改的权重数量，减少微调模型所需的工作量——不过工作方式很不同（LoRA 引入新的、更小的权重矩阵来“适配”现有冻结权重的结果，然后训练这些新矩阵）。 Raschka suggests an exercise where you try training all of the layers -- that is, with none of them frozen. I did that, and the results were really interesting -- more on that later... Raschka 建议做一个练习：尝试训练所有层，也就是不冻结任何层。我做了，结果非常有意思——稍后再说…… One thing that did surprise me a bit was that in this chapter we're training with [dropout](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/03/llm-from-scratch-10-dropout) of zero. It seems strange, but I think it's because we're freezing those layers. The number of parameters that are actually being trained is small, so dropping them out might just throw away signal from the training, and make it converge more slowly. What's worse is that there's nothing stopping dropout from happening in those frozen layers, too -- we've set `requires_grad` to `False`, so they're not being updated by the training loop, but the model is still in training mode, so dropout would happen in them if it wasn't set to zero. 有一点确实让我有些惊讶：本章训练时 dropout 设为零。这看起来很奇怪，但我想是因为我们冻结了那些层。实际训练的参数数量很少，丢弃其中一部分可能只是丢掉训练信号，让收敛更慢。更糟的是，冻结层也没有什么能阻止 dropout 发生——我们已将 requires_grad 设为 False，训练循环不会更新它们，但模型仍处于训练模式，因此如果不把 dropout 设为零，它们仍会执行 dropout。 Anyway, the code to actually run the training is pretty simple and I won't repeat what is already explained perfectly well in the book. My train (with whatever the differences with the seed it had from Raschka's) came out with broadly similar results: 无论如何，真正运行训练的代码很简单，书中已经解释得非常好，我就不重复了。我的训练（随机种子与 Raschka 的有所不同）得到的结果大致相近： ``` Training accuracy: 97.12% Validation accuracy: 95.97% Test accuracy: 95.67% ``` It took 15 seconds on my RTX 3090 -- within the "less than half a minute" range he mentions for the V100 and A100 datacenter cards. Plotting the loss: 在我的 RTX 3090 上耗时 15 秒——处在他所说 V100 和 A100 数据中心卡“不到半分钟”的范围内。绘制损失图： ![Loss over time training just the last layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/last-layers-loss-plot.png "Loss over time training just the last layers") ...you can see that it looks very similar to what happens in the book. ……可以看到，它与书中的情况非常相似。 The accuracy was kind of interesting, though: 不过准确率有点意思： ![Accuracy over time training just the last layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/last-layers-accuracy-plot.png "Accuracy over time training just the last layers") You can see that mine actually dropped off on the validation set near the start -- however, it did recover nicely, so no big deal. It looks like the best results were in somewhere around epoch 4, but there's not a huge drop off from there to where we stop at the end of epoch 5. [1](#fn-1) 可以看到，我的验证集准确率在开始附近实际上下降了——但很快漂亮地恢复，所以没什么大不了。最佳结果似乎出现在第 4 个 epoch 左右，不过从那里到第 5 个 epoch 结束时停止，下降幅度并不大。[1](#fn-1) The final results were a little disappointing, though. In the last pages of the chapter, we run two sentences through our trained classifier. Firstly, something that is very spammy: 不过最终结果有点令人失望。本章最后几页让我们用训练好的分类器运行两个句子。首先是非常像垃圾邮件的一句： ``` You are a winner you have been specially selected to receive $1000 cash or a $2000 reward ``` And secondly something that isn't spammy: 其次是一句不像垃圾邮件的： ``` Hey, just wanted to check if we're still on for dinner tonight? Let me know! ``` Unfortunately, due to the differences in seeding between my model and the one Raschka was working with, I got the same result for both: `not spam`. 遗憾的是，由于我的模型与 Raschka 使用的模型随机种子不同，两个句子都得到相同结果：not spam。 After checking the code carefully, I decided to take a look at what the actual predictions looked like; in the `classify_review` function that we write to do these tests, I added this: 仔细检查代码后，我决定看看实际预测是什么样；在我们为这些测试编写的 classify_review 函数中，我加入了： `print(torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1))` For the ham case, this printed: 对于正常邮件情况，输出是： ``` tensor([[0.9771, 0.0229]], device='cuda:0') ``` The first element (index 0) is the probability that it is predicting for ham, and the second is the probability for spam. So it was 97% sure that the ham message was indeed ham. That's good! 第一个元素（索引 0）是模型预测为正常邮件的概率，第二个是预测为垃圾邮件的概率。因此，它有 97% 的把握认为这条正常邮件确实是正常邮件。很好！ For the spam message, though, it was pretty much on the fence: 但对于垃圾邮件，它几乎处于五五开： ``` tensor([[0.5987, 0.4013]], device='cuda:0') ``` It thought that there was a 59.87% chance that it was ham, but a 40.13% chance that it was spam. It would be interesting to know what Raschka's own train came up with, but I can imagine that it might be a similarly close-run thing, and I was just unlucky with the way the randomness in training fell out. 它认为这条消息有 59.87% 的概率是正常邮件，40.13% 的概率是垃圾邮件。要是知道 Raschka 自己的训练结果会怎样一定很有趣，不过我可以想象他的结果可能也很接近，只是训练中的随机性恰好让我运气不好。 But I decided to try training all of the layers to see if I got any different results. 但我决定尝试训练所有层，看看结果是否不同。 ### Training all of the layers 训练所有层 This took 42 seconds rather than 15 -- hardly a big deal at this scale, but you can see how not having to train everything and getting a 3x speedup would be worthwhile for larger models. 这次耗时 42 秒，而不是 15 秒——在这个规模上并不算什么，但你可以看出，对于更大的模型，无需训练所有部分、获得 3 倍加速会很值得。 The results were definitely better, though: 不过结果确实更好： ``` Training accuracy: 99.71% Validation accuracy: 98.66% Test accuracy: 97.67% ``` Maybe a little bit of overfitting going on? But the important thing is that the validation and test samples' accuracy are higher too, we're not just memorising the training set. 也许有一点过拟合？但重要的是，验证和测试样本的准确率也更高，我们不只是记住训练集。 The loss graph also looks solid: 损失图也很扎实： ![Loss over time training all layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/all-layers-loss-plot.png "Loss over time training all layers") And accuracy is really interesting: 准确率更有意思： ![Accuracy over time training all layers](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-23-fine-tuning-classification/all-layers-accuracy-plot.png "Accuracy over time training all layers") You can see that validation accuracy got up to 100% sometime during the first epoch, lining up with the point where the loss plateaus! Perhaps a snapshot taken then would have been the best form of the model. 可以看到，验证准确率在第一个 epoch 的某个时刻达到了 100%，恰好与损失趋于平台的时刻一致！也许那时保存的模型快照才是最佳版本。 But anyway, I tried running the two samples from the last pages of the chapter through this new version of the model -- the results were exactly right! "You are a winner..." was classified as spam, and "Hey, just wanted to check..." as ham. Looking at the predictions that my modification to the classification code printed out, things were even clearer. The spam had this: 不过，我还是让这个新版本的模型运行了本章最后几页的两个样本——结果完全正确！“You are a winner...” 被分类为垃圾邮件，“Hey, just wanted to check...” 被分类为正常邮件。查看分类代码修改打印出的预测，结果更加清晰。垃圾邮件的输出是： ``` tensor([[0.0285, 0.9715]], device='cuda:0') ``` A 97% chance that it was spam, which is excellent. 这表示它有 97% 的概率是垃圾邮件，非常好。 Looking at the ham message, it said this: 再看正常邮件，输出是： ``` tensor([[9.9968e-01, 3.2288e-04]], device='cuda:0') ``` That's a 99.9% chance that it's ham! 也就是说，它有 99.9% 的概率是正常邮件！ So that was a nice note to end on. Not only did I have results that showed that the classification worked -- the fact that it worked with just the 30 seconds of extra training that enabling gradients on all of the layers gave meant that it was unlikely that my original slightly-disappointing results were due to an error in the code -- it was, as I'd suspected, just a bit of bad luck with some randomness. 这是一个很好的收尾。不仅结果证明分类有效，而且只需额外训练 30 秒、启用所有层的梯度就能成功，这说明我最初略显失望的结果不太可能是代码错误造成的——正如我怀疑的，只是随机性带来的一点坏运气。 ### Wrapping up 总结 So, that's it for chapter 6! Classification with a decapitated LLM done and dusted. Next time, it's on to instruction fine-tuning -- something that I spent quite a lot of time on [last year](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning), so let's see if all that work will pay off. 第 6 章就这样结束了！斩首 LLM 的分类任务完成。下一步是指令微调——我[去年](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning)在这上面花了不少时间，看看那些努力是否会派上用场。 [Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-24-the-transcript-hack). [这是本系列下一篇文章的链接](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-24-the-transcript-hack)。 **Update**: I decided to see how easy it would be to do the same decapitation trick on a different LLM, one that I'd downloaded from Hugging Face. Turns out the answer is "[pretty easy](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/a-classifier-using-qwen3)". **更新**：我决定看看在另一个从 Hugging Face 下载的 LLM 上做同样的斩首技巧有多容易。答案是“[相当容易](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/a-classifier-using-qwen3)”。 * * * 1. I've been running a number of separate experiments -- will be writing them up shortly -- in which I store a checkpoint after each validation check, and keep a symlink updated to point to the one with the best validation loss. This feels like a good practice to me. [↩](#fnref-1) 我一直在做许多独立实验——很快会写出来——每次验证检查后保存一个检查点，并不断更新符号链接，使其指向验证损失最佳的那个。我觉得这是很好的实践。 [↩](#fnref-1)
